full_judgment:
5. During trial, the prosecution produced as many as 20 witnesses including the said Rifat Akon as approver (PW 5) and defence produced none. With the end of the examination of prosecution witnesses, the accused were examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, whereupon they again denied the charges and refused to adduce any evidence. After completion of the trial, the Tribunal by impugned judgment and order convicted all the three accused, namely Jalal, Biplob and Porash, under sections 302/120B/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them as aforesaid. Since Rifat was treated as approver, he was exonerated from the charges, but ordered to be kept in jail until disposal of the Juvenile Case. 

 21. PW 13 was an employee of Bhai-Bhai Hotel at the time of occurrence. He does not remember the day of occurrence but deposed that the occurrence took place at about 9-00 AM. Upon hearing 3/4 gun shots, he closed the shutter of the hotel. After 10/15 minutes, he went to the Sikder Store and found Mr Goswami lying on the floor. He subsequently heard from the employee of Sikder Store that Mr Goswami was killed by Jillur, Biplob and Rifat. He identified Jillur on the dock and Rifat in the court. In cross-examination by Biplob, he deposed that he did not tell the investigating officer about the presence of Biplob. He further deposed that the distance of Sikder Store and Bhai-Bhai Hotel is two shops, one is laundry and the other is doctor's shop, and the area where the occurrence took place was called Vuter Golli. He further deposed that since he did not know Biplob, there was no reason to give false evidence against him. 

 33. It appears from the evidences on record that though three persons, namely Jalal, Biplob and Rifat, were present at the place of occurrence, Rifat has been made approver pursuant to the provisions of section 337 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, accordingly, he deposed as State witness (PW 5). Besides, there are four confessional statements made by four accused (including two child-accused) under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure-however, we will not consider the confessional statements of Shantunu and Apon as they were children and tried separately before a Juvenile Court under the provisions of the Children Act 1974. Since they are not before us, we do not want to rely on their confessional statements as it might violate the principles of natural justice and might prejudice their case. On the other hand, before relying on the confessional statements of child-accused, we are obliged to examine whether they were recorded in compliance with the special procedures as made applicable by this court in recording the confessional statements of children, which we do not want to do in their absence. [See the judgments of this court in the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust vs Bangladesh" 22 BLD 206 = 7 BLC 85 and Jaibar Ali Fakir vs State, 28 BLD 627 = 61 DLR 208; see also Ali, Justice M Imman, 'Towards a Justice Delivery System for Children in Bangladesh', UNICEF (2010), Dhaka, Chapter- 6.4.6] 

 35. Mr Nakib Saiful Islam, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of this condemned prisoner, submits that the prosecution has not been able to prove the charges against Zalal beyond reasonable doubt and, as such, his conviction should not sustain. Alternatively, he submits that even if the charges are found to have been proved beyond reasonable doubt, the sentence of death imposed upon him should be commuted to life imprisonment considering his young age and the fact that he has been on death row for long time. Mr Momtaj Uddin Fakir, learned Addl. AG and Mr M Ejarul Haque, learned DAG, on the other hand, submit that there are enough evidence for the conviction and sentence to sustain and, as such, the same should not be disturbed by this court. 

 39. Therefore, it is clear that the depositions of PWs 3, 4 and 5 as to the killing of Mr Goswami by Jalal correspond each other and they are supported by the confessional statement of Jalal himself. Although Jalal may be convicted solely on the basis of his confessional statement as the same has been found to be voluntary and true, yet his confessional statement is strongly supported by the depositions of PWs 3, 4, 5 and 6, who are eye-witnesses to the occurrence, leaving no scope of reasonable doubt. In addition, the' evidences against him are also corroborated by the postmortem report (exhibit-14) and the depositions of doctor (PW 18) who conducted the post-mortem on the dead body of Mr Goswami. The four entry injuries as mentioned in the postmortem report also correspond to the four gun shots fired in the killing of which 3 (three) were caused by the shots fired by Jalal. This evidence is also corroborated by PW 18 in that he recovered four bullets from the dead body (which he handed over to police) and also supported by the inquest report (exhibit- 2) as prepared by PW 15. 

 40. Above evidences are so consistent with each other that we do not find any semblance of reasonable doubt against the position that it was Jalal who was in the killing group and killed Mr Goswami by firing three gun shots. There are also evidences that he participated in the conspiracy to kill Mr Goswami and unsuccessfully tried to kill him on two previous occasions. 

 41. Considering the above evidences on record, we are of the view that the prosecution has been successful in proving charges against Zalal @ Jillu beyond reasonable doubt and, as such, we do not find any reason at all to interfere with the conviction on him as given by the Tribunal below. 

 42. Now the sentence of death. It appears from the evidences on record that Zalal was a professional killer and according to the deposition of PW 5. he had reportedly committed murders before (“এই আসামীগন মেহেরুন্নেছা স্কুলের সামনে দুটি হত্যাকরে মর্মে শুনেছি।”) and used to carry two pistols with him. On the other hand, the killing in question is a preplanned and premeditated one and became successful in the 3rd attempt. Convict Jalal along with others committed this murder in broad day-light in front of several eye-witnesses. Besides, he fired three gun shots one after another on Mr Goswami from a point blank distance, which shows without any doubt that he is a cold-blooded murderer who fired three shots to make sure that his victim did not have any chance to survive. Therefore, considering the above aspect and the material evidences on record, we are of the view that a professional cold blooded killer like Zalal does not deserve any mercy from this court. Therefore, we are not inclined to commute his death sentence to life imprisonment as prayed submitted by the learned advocate appearing for him. 

 43. Thus, since the prosecution has been able to prove the charges against Zalal beyond reason- able doubt and there is no circumstance in the case' to commute his sentence, his conviction and sentence of death should sustain. Accordingly, Death Reference No. 103 of 2006 in respect of Zalal @ Jillu is accepted and Criminal Appeal No. 5070 of 2006 and Jail Appeal No. 1080 of 2006 as preferred by him are dismissed. 

 44. Mr Khandokar Mahbub Hossain, learned senior counsel (with Mr Shakhawat Hossain and Mr Sheikh Mohammad Ali, the learned advocates), appearing for this condemned prisoner, took serious objection to the conviction and sentence imposed on Biplob by the Tribunal. Learned advocate submits that there is no evidence on record suggesting that Bipfob shot fire on Mr Goswami or that he was present in the alleged conspiracy to kill Mr Goswami. Mr Hossain points out that the only evidences on record are that Biplob was merely present at the place of occurrence, but did not take any part in the killing. 

 Therefore, his mere presence should not even be treated as an act done in furtherance of common intention to kill Mr Goswami within the meaning of section 34 of the Penal Code. Therefore, he submits, since Biplob's participation in the conspiracy and active part in the killing have not been proved by sufficient evidence, he should be acquitted. He further argues that the identification of Biplob has also remained doubtful, as there were other Biplobs in the concerned locality rendering the conviction on him very unsafe. In sup- port of his submissions, he refers to some decisions of this court, such as State vs Ershad Ali Sikder 56 DLR 305, Belal Ahmed vs State 40 DLR 154 and Aminul Islam vs State 12 MLR 21 = 12 BLC 332. 

 45. Mr Momtaj Uddin Fakir, learned Addl. AGand Mr M Ejarul Haque, learned DAG, on the other hand, submit that there are enough evidence for the conviction and sentence to sustain and, as such, the same should not be disturbed in any way. 

 49. Yes, we are aware of the legal position that Biplob cannot be convicted on the basis of confessional statement of co-accused Jalal, but he may be convicted under section 34 of the Penal Code if it is found that his presence at the place of occurrence was not an innocent one and he was there as a member of the killing group to kill Mr Gowsami-even in the absence of direct evidence to the effect that be shot fire at Mr Gowsami. The eye-witnesses like PWs 3, 4 and 6 proved his such guilty presence. PW 3 deposed that when Mr Goswami fell down after the first fire, he saw Jalal and Biplob firing 2/3 shots and thereafter fled away (“পরবর্তীতে আসামী জিল্লু ও বিপ্লব আরো ২/৩ টি গুলি করে। আসামী জিল্লু, বিপ্লব ও রিফাত দৌড়িয়ে চলে যায়।”). Although this witness did not state in his 164 statement before the Magistrate that he saw Biplob shooting fire, the circumstantial evidences and other evidences on record prove his active participation in the killing. PW 3 also identified Biplob in clear terms saying that he used to know Biplob and others before. 

 50. The evidence of PW 3 is also corroborated by PW 4 (another eye-witness), who deposed that he saw Jalal, Rifat and Biplob standing near the mosque. He saw Jalal shooting at the back of Mr Goswami's neck and saw Rifat, Jalal and Biplob fleeing away. He further confirmed that Biplob and Jillur ran together towards right. In cross-examination by Biplob he, in clear terms, identified Biplob (“আসামী বিপ্লব এলাকার ছেলে তাকে ঘোরাফিরা করতে দেখেছি।”) PW 6, another eye-witness, also supported more or less the eye-witness versions of other witnesses, namely PWs 3, 4 and 5. This active participation of Biplob in the killing was also corroborated by the confessional statement of Jalal and Rifat (exhibits 13 and 5). These being the evidences on record, even if we hold for argument's sake that there is no direct evidence to the fact that Biplob shot fire at Mr Goswami, yet the active participation of Biplob in the killing has been proved beyond reasonable doubt bringing him within the mischief of section-34 of the Penal Code. 

 51. Further, there are evidences on record that four shots were fired at Mr Goswami, four corresponding entry injuries were found on his dead body and four bullets were recovered from his body. It is also on record that Jalal fired three shots at Mr Goswami. Therefore, the other bullet was shot either by Biplob or Rifat, they were the only persons who were associating Jalal at the relevant time. However, the evidences indicate that although there were three persons in the killing group, Rifat was standing a bit away from Jalal and Biplob. Although Jalal in his confessional statement stated that Biplob shot a fire, that cannot be the basis of his conviction as the same is not a substantive evidence so far as Biplob is concerned. However, the circumstances of the events as unfolded through the depositions of the prosecution witnesses as well as the confessional statements of the accused very strongly indicate that it must have been Biplob who fired the 4th gun shot at Mr Goswamias he was the only other person who was also carrying a pistol at the relevant time. Thus, even if we hold that there is no direct evidence that Biplob shot the 4th fire, there is ample evidence on record that his presence on the killing scene was not an innocent one. Rather, he was an active member of the killing team from the beginning to the end, in particular at the time of the occurrence. He was standing just behind Zalal and fled away with him and was carrying a pistol. Therefore, there is no doubt that he actively participated in the killing in furtherance of common intention, which is enough to bring him under the preview of section 34 of the Penal Code. 

 53. Therefore, it is evident from evidences on record that the presence of Biplob was not a mere presence as boldly suggested by Mr Hossain, rather his presence at the relevant time at the place of occurrence was to participate in the killing and, accordingly, he played a role although there is lakh of unambiguous direct evidence that he shot a gun fire. Thus, it is crystal clear that the presence of Biplob at the crime scence with Zalal was not a mere presence but an active participation in the killing to bring him within the mischief of section 34 of the Penal Code. 

 54. Now, the criminal conspiracy. It appears that although there is no clear evidence that Biplob was present at the place of conspiracy on 24-10-2002 and 25-10-2002, there is ample evidence that he was all along active along with Zalal from the beginning to the end to kill Mr Goswami. Section 10 of the Evidence Act provides that when there is reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together to commit an offence or an actionable wrong, any-thing said, done or written by anyone of such persons in reference to their common intention, after the time when such intention was first entertained by anyone of them, is a relevant fact as against each of the persons believed to be so conspiring, as well as for the purpose of proving the existence of the conspiracy as for the purpose of showing that any such person was a party to it. 

 55. There is ample evidence that there was a conspiracy by two or more persons to kill Mr Goswami and on two occasions, namely on 24- 10-2002 and 25-10-2002, they conspired to kill him. We have already held that Biplob have all along played a roll in the two failed attempts to kill Mr Goswami and in the actual killing pursuant to the said conspiracy. Therefore, those acts leading to the actual killing done by him are enough to bring him within the per view of criminal conspiracy as defined by section 120A of the Penal Code with the help of section 10 of the evidence Act, if both are read together. 

 56. Conspiracy is done in secret. It is not possible to prove conspiracy by direct evidence. It has to be proved by circumstantial evidences. Considering this aspect, the legislators enacted section 10 of the Evidence Act. Here, there is evidence on record that there was conspiracy to kill Mr Goswami and pursuant to that conspiracy Biplob was actively present in two unsuccessful attempts to kill Mr Goswami and finally he actively participated in the real killing. Therefore, the conspiracy agency under section 10 of the Evidence Act will come into play to prove that there was existence of conspiracy and reasonable ground exists for believing that Biplob joined that conspiracy (see the illustrations to section 10 of the Evidence Act). This being so, we are of the view that the prosecution has also been able to prove the charge of conspiracy as punishable section 120B of the Penal Code against Biplob beyond reasonable doubt. 

 58. Now the sentence of death. It appears from the charge-sheet that the age of Biplob was mentioned as 17 and that there was no criminal record against him apart from the instant case. It further appears that though Biplob became a member of the criminal group led by Zalal and got involved in criminal activities like extortions, the present case is the first on his part so far as killing a human being is concerned. Unlike Zalal, since there is no evidence on record that Blplob is a professional killer, rather, there is evidence that he was a youth of tender age at the time of the commission of the offence and has been for long time on death row, we are of the view that his sentence of death should be commuted to the sentence of life imprisonment. 

 59. Accordingly, the Death Reference No. 103 of 2006 in respect of Maksudur Rahman Biplob is rejected. The Criminal Appeal No. 5103 of 2006 and Jail Appeal No.1 020 of 2006 as preferred by him are dismissed with the modification of death sentence on him to the sentence of life imprisonment. 

 60. Evidences on record, In particular the deposition of PW S(approver), shows that Porash was not a privy to the conspiracy concerned or that he did not do any act pursuant to such conspiracy (“স্যারকে হত্যা করবে পরিকল্পনার বিষয়ে আসামী পরাশ জানিতো না”) On the other hand, one of the attempts to kill Mr Goswami was not successful as because Porash and two others got scared, There is also evidence that only three persons, namely Zalal, Biplob and Rifat, took part In the killing on the day of occurrence. Considering this aspect of evidences on record, we are of the view that the prosecution has not been able to prove the charges against this convict beyond reasonable doubt and, as such, it will be unsafe to convict him. 

 61. With the above finding and analysis of the evidences, we conclude our judgment and order with the following result: 

 a) Death Reference No.103 of 2006 in respect of Zalal alias Zillu is accepted and Criminal Appeal No. 5070 of 2006 and Jail Appeal No. 1081 of 2006 as preferred by him are dismissed. 

 b) Death Reference No. 103 of 2006 in respect of Maksudur Rahman Biplob is rejected and Criminal Appeal No. 5103 of 2006 and Jail Appeal No.1020 of 2006 as preferred by him are dismissed with the modification of sentence in that the sentence of death on him be commuted to the sentence of life imprisonment. The concerned jail authority is directed to withdraw Maksudur Rahman Biplob from the condemned cell and keep him in the general prison.
